source.title: SGA: Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Step Forecasting in Time Series Foundation Models
source.authors: Xin-Miao Hu; Shuang Liang; Cheng Feng; Shao-Qun Zhang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a scale-related result for uncertainty estimates in time-series forecasting, but does not test the stated language-model loss scaling claims or rely on them as a tool.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the language-model scaling-law literature and says larger TSFMs tend to have lower predictive errors, but it does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, fit power laws to loss, test extrapolation from smaller language-model runs, or evaluate compute-optimal allocation. Its own uncertainty-versus-scale result is recorded as a related finding, not as a result for a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes an uncertainty-quantification method (SGA) for time-series foundation models (TSFMs). Its only scale result is a qualitative figure: larger TSFMs sit lower on uncertainty and ARMASE. It fits no power law and measures no pretraining loss. Model sizes are not controlled or stated, and there is no extrapolation, allocation or shape analysis. Kaplan et al. is cited only to say the accuracy trend is 'consistent with the scaling law'. So it tests no version, V5 and V6 included.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that larger-scale TSFMs typically produce lower multi-step forecast uncertainty estimates, which they call an 'empirical scaling law' of uncertainty. They also say larger TSFMs' lower forecast error is 'consistent with the scaling law of model performance' (citing Kaplan et al.). Both trends are not consistently visible on every individual dataset. The paper's main conclusion, though, is that SGA outperforms existing UQ methods in ranking forecast errors.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures forecast uncertainty in time-series foundation models; it does not reproduce the original language-model loss-scaling measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 11 TSFMs averaged over 27 datasets, larger-scale models tend to show lower SGA uncertainty estimates and lower ARMASE (Fig. 3). The pattern does not hold on every individual dataset (Fig. 7). No power-law fit or parameter counts are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger time-series foundation models tend to give lower multi-step forecast uncertainty estimates and lower forecast error, with the association varying across datasets.

record.problems: The scale-uncertainty relationship is presented in figures without exact uncertainty values, parameter counts, or fitted exponents. The authors note that the pattern is not consistently observable on every individual dataset.
record.rows_left_out: No other results bearing on the claim were reported. UQ method comparisons, ablations, and sensitivity analyses concern the proposed uncertainty-quantification method rather than the language-model scaling claims.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling law' language is loose: there is no functional fit, and model sizes are not reported. Chronos-T5 sizes are known only by name (Tiny to Large). The ARMASE baseline is normalised within each family. The only quantitative tables (NEAURC, overlap ratios) concern the UQ method, not scaling.

rows.subject: 11 TSFMs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Diverse scales; exact parameter counts not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Compared averaged uncertainty estimates and ARMASE across TSFMs of different scales.
rows.value: figure only; text reports that larger-scale TSFMs tend to have lower uncertainty estimates and lower predictive errors
rows.note: The paper describes this aggregate trend as an empirical scaling law for TSFM forecast uncertainty; it does not report fitted exponents or a power-law fit.
rows.check: The baseline is not 'not stated'. ARMASE is MASE relative to the smallest model of each family (C-T5-Tiny for Chronos-T5, C-2-Small for Chronos-2), aggregated by geometric mean (App. B.1). This makes cross-family comparisons of scale hard to read. Parameter counts are never given, and the result is read from a figure only. The state applies to the study's own uncertainty-vs-scale finding, not to any claim version.

rows.subject: TSFMs across individual datasets
rows.size_stated: Diverse scales; exact parameter counts not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Examined uncertainty estimates and MASE across model scales for individual datasets.
rows.measure: Whether larger-scale models trend toward lower uncertainty and lower MASE
rows.value: figure only; text says the trend is not consistently observable on every individual dataset
rows.note: The authors specifically note datasets where larger-model points do not lie in the lower-left direction relative to smaller-model points.
rows.check: Per-dataset plots (Fig. 7) show the trend is 'not consistently observable with every single dataset'. No counts of datasets are given. The row is correctly unlinked.
